passage: Monday. In the school corridor, some classmates laughed at Noor's faded uniform and said, "Her mother stitches for our mothers." Noor kept walking, jaw tight, and ate lunch in the library. Wednesday. Noor finally told Anirban, the class teacher, what had been happening for weeks. Anirban put down his pen. "Thank you for telling me. That's not right, and it's not your fault. I believe you." Anirban asked what would help, and Noor said, "Please don't make it a big scene." Friday. In class Anirban spoke about respect for every kind of work and every family, without naming anyone. At lunch a classmate, Neha, dropped her bag beside Noor. "Can I sit here?" Noor nodded, surprised by the lightness in her chest.

qa.q: Where did Noor eat lunch on Monday?
qa.a: Noor ate lunch in the library on Monday.

qa.q: How did Noor feel while walking away on Monday, and what shows it?
qa.a: Noor felt hurt and humiliated. Noor's jaw was tight and lunch was eaten in the library to avoid the classmates.

qa.q: What turning point on Wednesday changed things?
qa.a: Noor told Anirban what had been happening, and Anirban said it was not Noor's fault and believed Noor, which led to the class talk on Friday.

qa.q: How might Neha have seen Noor when asking to sit down?
qa.a: Neha may have noticed Noor eating alone and wanted to include Noor. Asking permission shows respect rather than pity.

grounding: A teenager is mocked for a faded uniform and family work, then is believed and supported by a teacher and a classmate.

passage: Leela, you asked why I always keep one extra chair at my table. Sit, I'll tell you. I am Ira, and at fifteen I was invited to Sunita's birthday. When I arrived, Sunita's aunt looked at my surname on the gift tag and said, "The seats are all taken." Everyone else was sitting. I stood holding the parcel while my face burned. Then our teacher Mr. Verma, who was a guest, said, "Then let us bring another chair," and carried one over himself. On Monday he asked me quietly whether I was all right and said, "I saw it. It was wrong, and you did nothing to deserve it." I still remember that chair. The next week Sunita came to my house with her mother, who apologised. So now I keep a chair.

qa.q: What did Sunita's aunt say when Ira arrived?
qa.a: Sunita's aunt looked at the surname on the gift tag and said, "The seats are all taken."

qa.q: How did young Ira feel standing with the parcel?
qa.a: Ira felt humiliated and hurt. Ira's face burned as everyone else sat while Ira stood.

qa.q: What choice did Mr. Verma make at the party that changed the moment?
qa.a: He said they would bring another chair and carried one over himself, treating the problem as easy to solve and not making Ira feel like a burden.

qa.q: How might Sunita's mother have felt when she came to apologise?
qa.a: Probably ashamed of what happened and wanting to make it right. Coming to the house shows she took it seriously.

grounding: A teenager is denied a seat because of a surname, and a teacher and later a host family recognise it as wrong and support the wounded teenager.

passage:
"Manoj Sir, can I talk to you?"
"Of course, Mahima. What's wrong?"
"The boys in my section keep saying my surname like a joke. They do an accent. Today someone wrote it on the board with a broom next to it."
"On the board? Today?"
"Yes. Everyone laughed. Even Shruti, and she's my friend."
"That must have hurt a lot."
"I'm fine."
"You're shaking, Mahima. You don't have to be fine."
"...It's been since Class 8. I stopped wearing my bangles because they said those too were 'village.'"
"Thank you for telling me. I believe you. This is discrimination, and it is not your fault. I'm going to the principal now, and I'll speak to your section this afternoon. Can I call your mother too?"
"Yes."
"And Mahima? Come to me any time. I mean it."

qa.q: What did someone draw next to Mahima's surname on the board?
qa.a: Someone wrote it on the board with a broom next to it.

qa.q: How can you tell Mahima felt more hurt than she said?
qa.a: She says she's fine but she is shaking, and she reveals it has gone on since Class 8 and made her stop wearing her bangles.

qa.q: What did Manoj Sir do right?
qa.a: He listened, said he believed her, named it as discrimination and not her fault, went to the principal and her section that day, and offered to call her mother.

qa.q: How might Shruti see what happened if she thought about it later?
qa.a: Shruti might feel guilty for laughing along and realise that her friend was deeply hurt, not just teased.

grounding: A teenager mocked for her surname and dress is believed and supported by a teacher who acts the same day.

passage:
In Class 9, Indu from my class had a birthday party, and everybody from our group was invited except me. I heard about it in the bus, everyone planning what to wear.
Later I found out why. Indu's mother had asked about my father's work. When she heard he repaired shoes near the market, she said, "Not that boy."
I didn't tell anyone for a week. I just stopped sitting with the group.
Then Indu herself found me. She said her mother was wrong and she was sorry. She'd already told our class teacher, and the teacher called me in the same afternoon. The teacher said, "Hemant, your father's work is honest. Anyone who says otherwise is the one who's wrong." And she asked if I wanted my parents in for a talk.
I'm in college now. I still remember that week. And I remember Indu choosing me.

qa.q: What was Hemant's father's work?
qa.a: He repaired shoes near the market.

qa.q: What was Hemant feeling during the week he didn't tell anyone?
qa.a: He felt hurt and ashamed, pulling away from his group after being left out because of his father's work.

qa.q: What made Indu's and the teacher's response helpful?
qa.a: Indu apologised and told the teacher, who called Hemant in the same afternoon, said his father's work is honest and offered a talk with his parents.

qa.q: How might Indu have felt about her mother's words?
qa.a: Indu likely felt embarrassed and troubled, and determined to set it right by choosing Hemant and telling the teacher.

grounding: A teenager left out of a party because of his family's work feels a lasting hurt and is supported by a peer and a teacher.

subtopic: Caste and class awareness, discrimination recognition and fair conduct
passage:
Class teacher's note, Class 10, 14 August.
At lunch today, Trisha came to the table where she usually sits with four girls. One of them put her bag on the empty chair and said, "This seat is for people who don't live in the basti." The others laughed. Trisha stood holding her tiffin, looking at the floor.
Jatin, from the next table, stood up and offered his chair. "Sit here." Trisha sat. She didn't eat.
I spoke with Trisha privately after lunch. She said it happens most days, about her home and her uniform. I told her I believed her and that she had done nothing wrong. With her permission I informed her mother and our counsellor the same afternoon.
I spoke separately to the girl who blocked the seat and to her parents. I also thanked Jatin. I will seat Trisha where she chooses tomorrow and check in each day.

qa.q: Who offered Trisha a chair?
qa.a: Jatin, from the next table, stood up and offered his chair.

qa.q: What does Trisha not eating suggest?
qa.a: It suggests she felt deeply hurt and humiliated after being denied the seat and laughed at.

qa.q: How did the teacher support Trisha well?
qa.a: The teacher believed her, said she had done nothing wrong, told her mother and the counsellor that day, spoke to the girl and her parents, and planned daily check-ins.

qa.q: How might Jatin see what happened at the table?
qa.a: Jatin clearly saw it as unfair and cruel, so he acted quickly to give Trisha a place to sit.

grounding: A teacher's note shows a teenager denied a seat because of where she lives, and how being believed and supported by a teacher and a peer matters.

passage:
Thursday night.
Today in the lab Kunal put his bag on the empty stool and said, loud enough, "Not for you, Saurabh. Your lot clean drains, go stand over there." Two others laughed. I stood by the sink for the whole practical. My face was burning and my hands were cold. Dad has fixed the school's pipes for years. I am proud of him, and I still wanted to disappear.
Jeevan saw everything. After the bell, Jeevan walked with me straight to Mrs. Pillai's desk and said, "Ma'am, something happened in the lab that you need to hear." She listened to all of it, wrote it down and said, "I believe you. This is about what they said, not about you." She phoned Kunal's parents before the last period and is changing the seating plan from tomorrow.
Still feels heavy. But I was believed.

qa.q: Where did Saurabh stand for the whole practical?
qa.a: Saurabh stood by the sink for the whole practical.

qa.q: What was Saurabh feeling in the lab, and what shows it?
qa.a: Saurabh felt humiliated and hurt, with a burning face and cold hands, wanting to disappear while still proud of Dad.

qa.q: What did Jeevan do that a good friend could copy?
qa.a: Jeevan did not just sympathise later but went with Saurabh to the teacher straight after the bell, so the report was made the same day with a witness.

qa.q: How does Mrs. Pillai see what happened?
qa.a: She treats it as serious wrongdoing by the others, not Saurabh's fault: she believes the account, writes it down, phones Kunal's parents and changes the seating.

grounding: It illustrates a teenager mocked and refused a seat over family work, and how a peer and a teacher who believe and act support them.
